p.seg: Of the god-king Gao Yang I am the far offspring,17
my late honored sire bore the name of Boyong.18
The sheti stars aligned with the year’s first month;19
gengyin was the day that I came down.20
He scanned and he delved into my first measure,21
from the portents my sire bestowed on me fine names:22
The name that he gave me was Upright Standard;
and my formal title was Numinous Poise.23
Hastening went I, as though I could not catch them—29
Such bounty I had of beauty within,26
this was doubled with fair appearance.27
I wore mantles of lovage and remote angelica,28
strung autumn eupatorium to hang from my sash.
I feared the years passing would keep me no company.
At dawn I would pluck magnolia on bluffs,30
In the twilight on isles I culled star anise blooms.31
Days and months sped past, they did not long linger,
springtimes and autumns altered in turn.
I thought on things growing, on the fall of their leaves,32
and feared for the Beauty, her drawing toward dark.
You do not cling to your prime and forsake what is rotting—33
why not change this measure of yours?34
I will drive my fine steeds, go off at a gallop—
I will now take the lead, in the vanguard chariot.35
The Three Kings of old were pure and unblemished,36
all things of sweet scent indeed were there.
Shen’s pepper was mixed together with cassia,37
while angelica, basil were not strung alone.38
Such shining grandeur had kings Yao and Shun;39
they went the true way, they found the path.
Why were kings Jie and Zhow slouching and shambling?—40
they walked at hazard on side-paths.41
Those men of faction had ill-gotten pleasures,44
their paths went in shadow, narrow, unsafe.
Not for myself came this dread of doom—
I feared the great chariot soon would be tipped.45
I went swiftly dashing in front and behind,46
till I came to the tracks of our kings before.
Lord Calamus did not fathom my nature within,47
he believed instead slander, he glowered in rage.48
I knew well my bluntness had brought me these ills,51
yet I bore through it, I could not forswear.
I pointed to Heaven to serve as my warrant,52
it was all because of the Numinous One.53
To me at first firm word had been given,54
she regretted it later, backed off, and was otherwise.55
I made no grievance at separation between us,
but was hurt that the Numinous One so often changed.56
I watered my eupatorium in all their nine tracts,
and planted basil in one hundred square rods;
I made plots for paeonia and for the wintergreen,57
mixed with wild ginger and sweet angelica.
I wished stalks and leaves would stand high and flourish,
I looked toward the season when I might reap.
If they withered and dried, it would cause me no hurt,
I would grieve if such sweetness went rotting in weeds.58
Throngs thrust themselves forward in craving and greed,60
never fully sated in things that they seek.61
They show mercy to self, by this measure others,62
in them the heart stirs to malice and spite.
Such a headlong horse-race, each hot in pursuit,
is not a thing that thrills my own heart.
Old age comes on steadily, soon will be here,63
At dawn I drank dew that dropped from magnolia,
I fear my fair name will not be fixed firmly.
in twilight ate blooms from chrysanthemums shed.65
If my nature be truly comely, washed utterly pure,66
what hurt can I have in being long wan from hunger?67
I plucked tendrils of trees to knot white angelica,68
pierced fallen pistils of flowering ivy.69
I reached high to cassia for stringing basil,
and corded continuous coils of rope-vine.
Yes, I took as my rule those fair men of old,70
it was not the garb worn in the ways of our age.71
Though it did not agree with men of these days,
I would rest in the pattern that Peng and Xian left.72
Long did I sigh and wipe away tears,
sad that men’s lives have so many hardships.73
Though love of the fair was the halter that guided me,74
at dawn I was damned and by twilight, undone.75
Yes, I was undone for a sash hung with basil,76
I lengthened it further by picking angelica.77
Still my heart finds goodness in these—
though I die many times, I will never regret.
I reproach the Numinous One’s unbridled wildness,
never discerning what lies in men’s hearts.78
Women-throngs envied my delicate brows,
scurrilous songs claimed I found lewdness good.79
Of these times the firm folkways: to be artful in guile;
facing compass and square, they would alter the bore-hole.80
They forswear the straight line, go chasing the crooked;
rivals for false faces, such is their measure.81
A woe wells within me, in such despair,82
alone at an impasse in times such as these.
Best to die promptly, to vanish away,83
for I cannot bear to show myself thus.
The bird of prey does not go in flocks,
so it has been from times long ago.
How can square and circle ever be matched?—
what man can find peace on a way not his own?84
Bending one’s heart, quelling one’s will,
abiding faults found, submitting to shame,85
wearing pure white, death for the right—86
these indeed were esteemed by sages of old.
I regretted judging the course was not well discerned,87
long I stood staring, about to go back.
I will turn my coach ’round, retrace my path—
before I stray too far in my going.
I let my horses walk through eupatorium meadows,89
sped to pepper-tree hill, there rested the while.
I drew close, did not reach him, I met with fault-finding,
I withdrew to restore that garb I first wore.90
I fashioned lotus and caltrop to serve as my robe,
I gathered the lotus to serve as my skirt.
No one knows me, it is all over!—
but truly my nature has scent steadfastly sweet.91
High was my hat, above me it loomed,
my pendants were long of shimmering patterns.92
Fragrance and filth were all intermingled,93
my gleaming flesh only suffered no dwindling.
All at once I looked back, and I let my eyes roam,
I would go off to view the wild lands around.95
Pendants in profusion, I was richly adorned,
their sweet fragrance spread, ever more striking.
Each man has a thing in which he finds joy:
I alone love the fair, in that I abide.
Though my limbs be cut from me, I still will not change,96
how could my heart be subdued?97
Then came the Sister, tender and enticing,98
she said: “Gun was unyielding, he fled into hiding,100
at last died untimely on moors of Mount Yu.101
“Why such wide culling, such love of the fair,102
in you alone bounty of beautiful raiment?103
They stack stinkweed filling their rooms;104
you alone stand apart and will not wear it.105
“No swaying the throngs person by person;106
‘no one discerns this my nature within’!107
Men now rise together, each favors their own ilk,
why do you stand alone and not listen to me?”
I trust sages of old for fair judgment,108
my heart swelled in rage, it had come now to this.109
I crossed Xiang and Yuan, faring on southward,
reached Chonghua, to state him my case:110
“King Qi had Nine Variations and the Nine Songs—111
extreme in wild pleasures, he did as he pleased.112
He was heedless of troubles, made no plans for the morrow,
whereby the five sons brought strife to his house.113
“Yi roamed recklessly, he was lavish in hunts,114
he also loved shooting the great foxes.115
Indeed, going cross-current rarely ends well:116
and Han Zhuo was lusting to seize his bride.117
“Guo Ao garbed himself, he opposed violently;118
he followed his wants, he failed to forbear.
He lost himself daily in wild pleasures.119
whereby his own head was toppled and fell.
“Xia’s Jie was constant in his erring,120
in pursuit of these he met with his doom.121
Shang’s Zhow, the Lord Xin, minced men into stew,122
whereby Yin’s great lineage could not last long.123
“Yu the Great was stern, respectful and godly;124
the right way was Zhou’s norm and thus did not stray.125
They raised men of worth, rewarded the able,
they kept the straight line, they did not veer.“
Sovereign Heaven is slanted in favor of none;
it scans a man’s virtues, puts helpers beside him.126
Only when sage wisdom does deeds that are splendid,
may one then be used in this land down below.127“
I viewed times before us, looked to times yet to come,
observed measures of men, and the ends of their plans:128
who found wanting in virtue may be put to use?
who found wanting in good may still be retained?129
“By the brink stands my body, I am in death’s peril,131
I scanned my beginnings and still regret not.
Not judging the drill-hole, they squared the peg:132
indeed fair men of old came to mince in a stew.”133
Sighs come from me often, my heart swells within,134
sad that my time was not right.
I pluck hare’s ear and basil to wipe away tears,135
that soak my gown’s folds in their streaming.
I knelt with robes open thus stated my case,
having grasped so clearly what is central and right.136
I teamed jade-white dragons, rode the Bird that Hides Sky,137
waiting for winds to fleetly fare upward.138
At dawn I loosed wheel-block there by Cangwu,139
and by twilight I reached the Gardens of Air.140
I wished to bide awhile by the windows of gods,141
but swift was the sun and it soon would be dusk.
I bade sun-driver Xihe, to slacken her pace,
to stand off from Yanzi and not to draw nigh.142
On and on stretched my road, long it was and far,
I would go high and go low in this search that I made.
I watered my horses in the Pools of Xian,143
and twisted the reins on the tree Fusang,144
snapped a branch of the Ruo tree to block out the sun,145
I roamed freely the while and lingered there.
Ahead went Wang Shu to speed on before me,146
behind came Fei Lian, he dashed in my train.147
Phoenix went first and warned of my coming,148
Thunder-master told me that all was not set.149
I bade my phoenixes to mount up in flight,
to continue their going both by day and by night.150
Then the whirlwinds massed, drawing together,
they marshaled cloud-rainbows, came to withstand me.151
A bewildering tumult, first apart, then merging together,
they streamed shimmering colors, high and then low.152
I bade the God’s gatekeeper to open the bar;
he stood blocking the gateway and stared at me.153
The moment grew dimmer, moonrise would be soon,154
I plait eupatorium, long stand fixed and gazing.155
An age foul and murky cannot tell things apart;
it loves to block beauty from malice and spite.
At dawn I set to ford across the White Waters,156
I climbed Mount Langfeng, there tethered my horses.157
All at once I looked back, my tears were streaming,
sad that the high hill lacked any woman.158
At once I went roaming to the Palace of Spring,159
I snapped stalks of qiong to add to my sash.160
Before the bloom’s glory had fallen away,
I would divine a woman below on whom to bestow them.161
Feng Long I bade to go riding the clouds,164
to seek out Fu Fei where she dwells.
I took pendant-sash, I tied there a message,
and bade Lady Blunt to act as my envoy.165
A bewildering tumult, first apart, then merging,166
she suddenly balked, she could not be swayed.167
and at dawn bathed her hair in Weiban Stream.169
She went twilights to lodge at Farthest-of-Rocks,168.
She held on to her beauty, she was scornful and proud,170
in wild pleasures daily she wantonly roamed.171
Though beautiful truly, she lacked right behavior—
Come, let her go then, I will seek for another.
I scanned and observed all the world’s ends,172
I roamed throughout sky, then I came down.
I viewed the rising crest of a terrace of onyx,
there saw a rare woman, the You-Song’s daughter.173
I bade the venom-owl to make match between us,174
the venom-owl told me it was not good.175
The dove-cock went away singing,176
and I still loathe its petty wiles.
My heart then faltered, doubts overcame me,
I wanted to go myself; it was not allowed.
Already the phoenix had given its gift,177
I feared that Gao Xin had come before me.178
I wanted to alight far away, there was no place to halt,
so I drifted the while and roamed at my ease.
My envoy was feeble, the matchmaker, bumbling;
If still not yet married to Shaokang the Prince,
there remained the two Yao girls of the clan You-Yu.179
I feared words to charm them would not hold fast.
An age foul and murky, it spites a man’s worth,
it loves to block beauty, it acclaims what is ill.180
Remote and far are the chambers of women;
and the wise king also is not yet aware.
I keep feelings within me, do not bring them forth,
yet how can I bear that it be thus forever?
I sought out qiong stems, for stalks to cast lots,
and bade Numinous Fen to divine the thing for me.182
He said: “Two lovely beings must surely be matched;183
whoever is truly fair adore her.184
“Consider the wide sweep of these Nine Domains—
can it be only here that a woman be found?”18
He said: “Undertake a far faring, be not full of doubts;
none who seeks beauty would let you slip by.186
“Is there any place lacking in plants of sweet fragrance?
why must you so cherish your former abode?187
This age is a dark one, eyes are dazzled and blinded,
no man can discern what I find good or hate.
“What men love and loathe is never the same—188
only these men of faction alone stand apart.189
Each person wears mugwort, stuffed in his waist,190
they declare eupatorium may never be strung.
“If in discerning plants they still cannot grasp it,
can they ever be right in judgments of beauty?191
They seek shit and mire to stuff their sachets,192
and say that Shen’s pepper lacks any sweet smell.”
I wished to follow Numinous Fen’s lot of good fortune,
yet my heart faltered, doubts overcame me.
Shaman Xian would descend in the twilight,
I clasped pepper and rice to beseech him.195
The gods blotted sky, their full array descending,
the hosts of Many Doubts joined to go greet him.196
Gloriously shining he sent forth his spirit,197
giving me word of fortunate outcomes.198
He said: “Undertake to fare high and then to fare low,199
seek one who agrees with the yardstick and square.200
Yu the Great was stern, he sought one who matched him,201
he held to Gao Yao as one able to suit him.202
“If one’s nature within loves what is fair,
what need to make use of matchmaker or envoy?
Yue held an earth-ram upon Fu’s cliff;203
Wuding employed him and did not doubt.
“Lü Wang swung the knife of a butcher,204
yet he met Zhou’s King Wen and he was raised up.
And there was Ning Qi, a singer of songs,
Huan of Qi heard him; he assisted in all.205
“Yet act now before the year grows too late,
now while the season has not yet passed.
I fear only cries early from summer’s nightjar,206m
aking all plants lose their sweet scent.”
My sash-hangings of qiong, how they dangle swaying—207
The times are in tumult, ever transforming.209
how then may a man linger here long?
Eupatorium, angelica change, they become sweet no more;
calamus and basil alter, they turn into straw.
How do sweet-smelling plants of days gone by
now become nothing more than stinking weeds?210
Can there be any reason other than this?—
the harm that is worked by no love for the fair.
I once thought Eupatorium could be steadfast:211
it bore me no fruit, it was all show.212
Forsaking its beauty, it followed the common;
it wrongly is ranked in the hosts of sweet scent.213
Pepper is master of fawning, it is swaggering, reckless,214
only mock-pepper stuffs sachets hung from waists.215
It pressed hard to advance, it struggled for favor,
what sweet scent remains that is able to spread?216
Truly, ways of these times are willful and loose,217
who now is able to avoid being changed?
Viewing eupatorium and pepper, seeing them thus,
will it be less true of lovage and wintergreen?
Only these my own pendants are still to be prized;
forsaken is beauty, and I come to this.218
Yet their sweet scent spreads, it is not diminished,
even now the aroma has still not abated.
In their blending’s measure I take my delight,219
I will drift and will roam, seeking the woman.
And while such adornment is still in its glory,
I will range widely looking, both high and low.
Since Numinous Fen told me my lot of good fortune,
I choose a day of good fortune, and I will set out.220
I snap stalks of qiong to serve as my viands,221
a fine qiong meal will serve as my fare.
For me have been hitched those dragons that fly,
mixed onyx and ivory serve as my chariot.
How can a mind set apart be ever like others?222
I will go away far, keep myself removed.
I bent my way round at Kunlun Mountain,
Long and far was the road, there I ranged all around.
I raised my cloud-rainbows, dimming and darkening,
jade phoenix chimes rang, with a jingling sound.
At dawn I loosed the wheel-block at Ford-of-the-Sky,223
by twilight I came to the ends of the west.
Phoenix spread its wings, and bore up my banners,
high aloft it soared, its wing-beats were steady.
All at once I was faring across Drifting Sands,
I went along the Red Waters, there took my ease.224
I signaled the dragons to make me a bridge,
I called to West’s Sovereign to take me across.
Long and far was the road, it was filled with perils,
I had all my chariots mount up, drive straight and attend me.225
I made my path to Mount Buzhou, there turned to the left,226
toward the Sea of the West my appointed goal.
Then I massed my chariots, a thousand strong,
jade hubs lined even, we galloped together.227
I hitched my eight dragons, heaving and coiling,
and bore my cloud banners streaming behind.
I then quelled my will and slackened my pace;228
they were playing Nine Songs and dancing the Shao,230
the gods galloped high far into the distance,229
making use of this day to take their delight.231
I was mounting aloft to such dazzling splendor—232
all at once I peered down to my homeland of old.
they flexed looking backward and would not go on.233
My driver grew sad, my horses felt care,
The Ending Song:

It is done now forever!In the domain there is no one, no one who knows me,234then why should I cherish that city, my home?Since no one can join me in making beautiful rule,I will go off to seek where Peng and Xian dwell.235
